newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS - France seeks protocol to EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France seeks protocol to EMU budget pact.

text.p: France is seeking a protocol to complete the EU stability pact that will spell out how EU countries will coordinate economic policy after the launch of the euro, former European Commission president Jacques Delors said in an interview published on Monday.
Delors, who has been advising the new Socialist-led government, told the Belgian daily Le Soir that France was simply seeking the application of the Maastricht Treaty.

His comments tied in with those made on Sunday by new French Finance Minister Dominque Strauss-Kahn, who told reporters during a meeting of EU finance ministers he could not see how anyone would doubt France's commitment to meeting the timetable and criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Strauss-Kahn was due to spell out the French government's position on Monday, amid fears in some quarters it might take a tough line on Europe that could threaten the planned launch of the single currency in 1999.
"We are seeking the application of the (Maastricht) treaty, notably the provisions which aim to create an economic pillar alongside the monetary pillar," Delors said.

"Article 103 of the Maastricht Treaty foresees that every year the European Council adopts common policies on economic issues," Delors said. "We need to spell out how this will be done in a protocol which will complete the stability pact."

The Socialist party, swept to power in a surprise parliamentary election victory earlier this month, said during the campaign it wanted a European economic government alongside the future European Central Bank.
"The French government simply wants to respect the spirit and the letter of the treaty," Delors said.

To answer growing popular demands in Europe for greater emphasis on jobs and social protection, as much weighting must be given to the views of labour ministers as to those of finance ministers, he said.

His comments echoed those made on Sunday by Luxembourg Finance Minister Jean-Claude Juncker who pledged to use Luxembourg's presidency of the EU, which starts next month, to find ways of linking finance and social affairs ministers.
That would allow France to have what it calls an "economic government", Juncker said.
Delors said the stability pact, which would limit budget deficits after the launch of the single currency, was essential to ensuring sound economic policies would be maintained after 1999.
"But this stability pact must be completed through the co-ordination of economic policies. It is essential," he said.
EU ministers on Sunday played down any risk of a row over the stability pact, due to be approved by EU heads of state and government at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
Any attempt to renegotiate the pact could create a diplomatic crisis with Germany, which sees it as a guarantee of fiscal discipline after the launch of the euro in 1999.
"We can find the ways and means to reach an agreement in Amsterdam," said Juncker, whose coments were echoed by Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto.
Juncker said the pact was meant to ensure that the values of economic stability were enshrined in EMU.
"We have to see with the stability pact if we can reach an interpretation which suits everybody."

Economists suggested last week that France's new government could leave the body of the stability pact intact while insisting on adding some new wording to place the emphasis on fighting for growth and employment.
It could also look for further moves towards a European economic government which would draw up policies for the euro zone designed to boost growth and lower unemployment.
The Socialist party made the fight for jobs and growth in Europe a key plank of its election campaign.

The previous centre-right government had also fought for an economic government, but after running into opposition from some of its EU partners, agreed in the end on an informal stability council to co-ordinate policies in the euro zone.
